newsitem.title: UK: War reporter goes into UK political battle.
newsitem.headline: War reporter goes into UK political battle.

text.p: Veteran BBC war reporter Martin Bell went nervously into political battle on Monday, saying his decision to stand as an "anti-corruption" candidate in Britain's election campaign could be the biggest mistake of his life.

Bell, one of Britain's most respected television journalists, stepped forward as an independent candidate with backing from the main opposition parties to take on a former Conservative government minister accused of taking cash for asking questions in parliament on behalf of businessmen.
Bell, who reported from the front lines of 11 wars in a trademark white suit, said he expected his political career to last no longer than a few days.
"I am deeply nervous. It could be the biggest mistake of my life," Bell, 58, told Reuters in an interview before facing the other side of the cameras at a 1330 GMT press conference.

Candidates of the main opposition parties, Labour and the Liberal Democrats, have agreed to stand aside unless Conservative MP Neil Hamilton, who denies the allegations against him, withdraws from the race in his Tatton constituency in north-west England.

Bell's entry as a single candidate against him would allow the opposition to combine their votes against him and appeal for non-partisan support from Conservatives unhappy with Hamilton's refusal to quit.

"I am hoping to clear the air, to apply that little bit of pressure to get him (Hamilton) to stand down and then I will be out of it," said Bell, who was wounded by shrapnel while reporting from Bosnia in the early 1990s.
"I think it's going to be the shortest career in British political history." Hamilton faces a constituency meeting on Tuesday when he will face pressure to stand down.

He said he had been approached by a friend with connections to both the Labour and Liberal Democrat parties, who have sought to capitalise on Conservative discomfort over a series of sex and money scandals.
"I think it is a good idea. I think I can make a difference," Bell said.
"I don't like sleaze. I am concerned about the effects of money in our society anyway...I think it has affected the political process and I think people are really turned off by it."
Bell's surprise decision was seen as a serious setback for the Conservatives, who are fighting an uphill battle to retain power after 18 years in office.

The right-wing Daily Express newspaper welcomed the news with a front-page story headlined "White Knight." Liberal Democrat leader Paddy Ashdown described Bell as a man of "the highest integrity and who commands overwhelming respect."
Bell was a Liberal campaigner while a student but said he dropped all political allegiances when joining the BBC in 1962. The BBC has given him leave to fight the election campaign.
Bell hung up his flak jacket last year and returned home declaring he had had enough of war reporting.
He has since criticised BBC policies of neutrality in reporting war and genocide, saying he did not believe journalists should stand neutral between good and evil.
But a political career on the front-line of an election campaign dogged by scandals over financial and personal morality could hardly have been further from his mind.
"I wouldn't have thought of doing this in a million years," he said. "I am probably going to accumulate some enemies for the first time in my life... It is flak of a different sort."
